title: Why Do Things Fall?
subtitle: A feather and a hammer, and what really makes things fall.

hook.title: Let go of something
hook.body:
Hold a pen in the air and let go. It falls. It has always fallen. Nobody ever had to teach you that, and you have never seen a pen float up on its own.

But why does it fall? The answer is a force that pulls every object towards the centre of the Earth. It is called gravity. In this lesson you will watch gravity at work, and then test a question people argued about for about two thousand years: does a heavy thing fall faster than a light thing?

drop.title: A ball falling
drop.body:
Here is a ball above the ground. Press Simulate and watch it. Next to the ball a graph draws its speed, and a second line draws its height.

Look at the speed line. It does not jump to a fixed value. It starts at zero and keeps climbing. The ball goes faster and faster every second while it falls. That steady speeding-up is called acceleration.

gravity.title: How fast does it speed up?
gravity.body:
On Earth, every falling object (with no air to slow it) gains about 9.8 metres per second of speed every second. We write this as g = 9.8 m/s² and call it the acceleration due to gravity.

So after 1 second the speed is about 9.8 m/s. After 2 seconds it is about 19.6 m/s. After 3 seconds, about 29.4 m/s. The rule is simple: speed = g × time.

predict.title: Heavy or light?
predict.body: Imagine two balls, one 1 kg and one 10 kg, let go from the same height at the same moment. There is no air to get in the way.

air.title: So why does a feather fall slowly?
air.body:
You have seen a feather drift down much more slowly than a stone. That is air, not gravity. A feather is wide and very light, so the air pushes up on it a lot compared with its tiny weight. This push is called air resistance (or drag).

On the Moon there is no air. When astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather together there in 1971, they landed at the same time. Try changing the mass of the ball below. The speed graph stays the same.

worked.title: How fast after 3 seconds?
worked.body: A stone is dropped off a bridge. How fast is it going after 3 seconds? (Ignore air.)
worked.steps: Write down what you know: the acceleration of gravity and the time. The stone starts from rest, so its speed is just g multiplied by the time. Multiply. Does the answer make sense? 29.4 m/s is about 106 km/h, which is fast, and that is why dropping things from a bridge is dangerous.
